rows.description: A teenager who receives a threat online or in person treats it seriously, avoids engaging, keeps a record and reports it to a trusted adult, school or authorities. A threat is not a challenge to be won.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager builds an argument with claims and evidence in class or at home and defends a view. Debate skill includes acknowledging good points; winning by volume or ridicule is a common pitfall.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager bargains for curfew, phone time or independence by offering trust-building steps. Calm proposals with a trial period tend to succeed better than arguing or sneaking around.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager faces persuasion to try risky things and can say no, suggest another plan, blame a rule or leave. A good friend accepts a refusal; repeated pressure is a reason to seek an adult or new company.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager tells a parent, teacher or counsellor about stress, mistakes or unsafe situations. Adults who listen first, stay calm and avoid instant punishment make later disclosure more likely.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager posts personal details or feelings publicly, sometimes seeking support or attention. Pausing before posting, considering permanence and audience, and using trusted friends for heavy topics protects privacy.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Revealing a feeling to a peer or crush [Mismatch]
rows.description: A teenager may hint at, joke about or partially reveal a feeling to test the response. Vulnerability is risky, and it is wiser to share with those who have shown care and respect.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager trades quick jokes with friends and uses shared references. Banter builds belonging but can exclude, and jokes that rely on stereotypes or someone's pain can harm even when framed as fun.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: playfulness, nostalgia, hurt

rows.description: A teenager shares memes, parodies and satirical clips to comment on school, politics or life. These convey shared attitudes economically, though satire may be mistaken for fact and can hurt if it mocks vulnerable people.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager says "Great, just great" meaning the opposite, using tone or a flat delivery. Sarcasm can signal frustration, humour or contempt, and in text or across cultures it is easily misread, so a clarifying "Are you joking?" is fair.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: amusement, anger, contempt
